title: Data-Driven Surrogate-Model for Real-Time Loads Prediction in Floating Wind Farms
summary: This work presents a data-driven load-surrogate modelling framework for real-time control of floating offshore wind farms. The proposed methodology uses mid-fidelity simulations performed with OpenFAST and FAST.Farm together with MLife fatigue analysis to generate Damage Equivalent Load (DEL) datasets of floating wind turbines under wake steering conditions. A two-stage surrogate modelling approach is adopted: first, a Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN) is trained using data from simulations of a single floating wind turbine, while a second stage corrects the residual error between the FFNN predictions and FAST.Farm simulations using either Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) or an additional FFNN. The results show that the proposed framework can estimate DELs with errors generally below 15% for tower base bending moment, blade root bending moment, yaw bearing moment, and fairlead tension, while maintaining computational times compatible with real-time applications. The study also highlights the challenges related to generalization of the load-surrogate model under varying environmental and control conditions, especially for large floating wind farms. Overall, the proposed methodology demonstrates the potential of surrogate-based DEL estimation for load-aware floating wind farm control applications.

title: Purpose IR: Compiling User Purpose for Privacy-Preserving Agent Workflow State
summary: LLM-agent workflows routinely transform rich observations into plans, summaries, memories, handoffs, and other reusable state. This creates a privacy boundary that task relevance alone does not capture: an observation may be needed as evidence for a task without its full semantics being authorized to persist. We call this mismatch the purpose-to-state semantic gap. The key distinction is that evidence authority is not release authority. We introduce Purpose IR, a bounded typed intermediate representation that compiles natural-language user purpose into an executable semantic boundary for reusable agent state. A Purpose program is an acyclic semantic dataflow graph in which evidence leaves specify task-required semantics, typed dependencies constrain authorized derivations, and declared sinks determine which values or actions may cross the reusable-state boundary. A deterministic compiler constructs and validates the authoritative program, while a typed runtime reconstructs reusable state only from validated sink outputs. Under explicit execution contracts, this design yields release confinement and purpose noninterference, characterizing what factual semantics may be released and which observation differences must become irrelevant to reusable state. Across 1,200 cases spanning LangGraph, CrewAI, and MobileRun, Purpose IR achieves 99.6% Privacy, 83.3% Task, and 83.3% Privacy-Compliant Success (PCS), outperforming the strongest high-privacy baseline by 27.5 PCS points. On 493 PrivacyLens trajectories, it achieves the highest Safe Action Rate at 77.3%, 10.4 points above the next-best method, extending the same boundary from reusable state to downstream actions. These results show that privacy-preserving agent state requires more than filtering sensitive or task-irrelevant content: it requires an explicit, executable representation of what the user's purpose authorizes to survive.

title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
summary: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.

title: SiteEvo: An LLM Agent for Autonomous Discovery of Site-Adaptive Massive MIMO Detectors
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Designing a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detector that is tailored to each specific deployment site can improve detection performance, yet most existing detectors, including deep-unfolding methods, adapt mainly within human-prescribed algorithmic structures. This letter proposes SiteEvo, a site-adaptive agentic discovery framework that extends adaptation from parameter tuning to detector-algorithm discovery. Rather than selecting or recombining predefined architectures, the large language model (LLM) agent synthesizes complete executable detector programs under a common design contract by combining its pretrained communication knowledge, site-specific wireless evidence, and experience accumulated during the search. Each proposal defines its own processing structure and trainable parameterization, and the parameters are optimized by a communication-system backend. The resulting high-performance detector is further structurally refined to reduce block-level computational cost under a bit error rate (BER)-preservation constraint and is finally frozen for deployment without online LLM inference. Simulations across three sites demonstrate BER reductions by factors of 2.6 to 6.0 over the best-performing competing detector at each site at 6 dB, while structural refinement reduces block-level computational cost by 16.7-34.1% under a validation-BER constraint.

title: Rarity Determines Minimax Rates of Semantic Entropy From Weak Pairwise Judgments With a Known Channel
summary: The semantic entropy of a language model is the entropy of the meanings of its sampled answers. The meanings are never observed, and the entropy is estimated from the verdicts of a pairwise equivalence judge. Given the meanings of $n$ answers, a known channel declares each pair equivalent independently, with probability $q+Δ$ within a meaning and $q$ across meanings. At most $K$ meanings occur, and $q$ is bounded away from $0$ and $1$. For a weak judge, with $nΔ^2\to0$, the global minimax rate is set by distributions near a vertex of the simplex and overstates the difficulty elsewhere. We show that the difficulty is set by how many meanings can be rare. Over distributions with at most $s$ meanings below a fixed probability $τ<1/(K-s)$, the minimax squared risk is of order $N^{-1/s}$ for $s\ge2$, $N^{-1}\log^2(e+N)$ for $s=1$ and $N^{-1}$ for $s=0$, capped at one, where $N=n^KΔ^{2K-2}$. The matching lower bounds hold on every fixed polynomial window $nΔ^2\le n^{-κ}$. One estimator attains these rates without knowing $s$ or $τ$: it averages products of centered verdicts along all spanning trees of every $k$-set of answers, projects the resulting power sums onto the valid moment set and inverts them. The case $s=K-1$ gives the global rate $N^{-1/(K-1)}$ and the consistency threshold: with $Δ=n^{-γ}$ the entropy is uniformly consistently estimable exactly when $γ<K/(2K-2)$. On polynomial windows, the same estimator attains the sharp local minimax constant on shrinking neighborhoods of interior points with distinct probabilities. Restricting the average to stars multiplies the constant by $K^{K-3}$.

title: Fast Analytical Method for Resource Adequacy Assessment in Renewable-Rich Power Systems
summary: This paper proposes a novel analytical method for resource adequacy assessment in renewable rich power systems. The approach begins by applying the stress strength method to estimate two key resource adequacy indices: loss of load expectation (LOLE) and expected energy not supplied (EENS). This method requires defining the probability distribution functions (PDFs) for both the generation side and the load side. The load is assumed to follow a normal probability distribution, while the generation side probability distribution is derived from the combined PDFs of conventional, wind, and solar power sources. The approach models the cumulative impact of uncertainties on resource adequacy using the central limit theorem (CLT), and improves accuracy with a cumulant based Gram Charlier expansion when the CLT alone is insufficient. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through Monte Carlo simulations conducted on the IEEE single area and multi-area RTS-96 test systems. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in computational time, which is crucial in the context of operational planning, without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, its performance improves as renewable penetration increases, making it particularly suitable for future power systems operation and planning.

title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
summary: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.

title: Design Choices for Multimodal Transformer Learning with Missing and Longitudinal Healthcare Data
summary: Multimodal learning offers the potential to improve predictions by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous data sources. However, multimodal datasets are frequently incomplete, raising important questions about how models should handle missing information. Although recent approaches increasingly rely on Transformer-based architectures for multimodal fusion, incomplete multimodal data introduces challenges such as missing modalities and intra-modal missingness, which motivate key architectural design choices, such as tokenization granularity. In addition, many datasets are longitudinal, with observations collected across multiple time points. The sequential nature of the Transformer architectures provides a natural framework for modeling such data, but introduces additional considerations, such as how temporal information should be represented. In this study, we systematically investigate these design choices using three different cancer datasets. We compare modality-level and feature-level tokenization and evaluate attention masking and imputation as strategies for handling missing information, both naturally occurring in the datasets and synthetically induced. We further investigate approaches for incorporating temporal information in our training process and how to model it. Experiments are conducted with unimodal and multimodal configurations, as well as different levels of missingness for binary survival classification and multiple time encoding strategies for discrete-time survival prediction. Our results show that while multimodal outperforms unimodal results, missing data heavily impacts predictions and thus effective design choices such as tokenization granularity, and intra-missing handling is essential for reliable prediction.

title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
comment: This paper has been accepted in The 14th IEEE Conference on Communications and Network Security (IEEE CNS 2026)
summary: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal. The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.

title: The Gauss--Newton Method for Phase Retrieval from Coded Diffraction Patterns
summary: We study the minimum-norm Gauss--Newton method for phase retrieval from random coded diffraction patterns with additive intensity noise. For bounded symmetric masks satisfying the standard complex moment conditions, we establish convergence guarantees with quadratic error recursions in both the resampled and fixed-data settings. In the resampled setting, $O(\log^2 n)$ masks per independent block suffice to obtain a spectral initializer within a constant-relative-radius neighborhood and to establish a local quadratic error recursion with an additive noise term. Consequently, in the noiseless case, the method achieves relative accuracy $ε$ using $O(\log\log(1/ε)\log^2 n)$ masks. In the fixed-data setting, $O(\log^6(en))$ masks suffice for spectral initialization within a neighborhood whose relative radius is proportional to $\log^{-5/2}(nL)$. Within this neighborhood, the method satisfies a linear contraction bound and eventually a quadratic error recursion. In particular, in the noiseless case, the method initially converges linearly and enters a quadratic convergence phase after $O(\log n)$ iterations, without acquiring additional masks. Numerical experiments on synthetic signals and a natural image demonstrate the method's efficiency relative to state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: On Over-Conservatism Under Low-Probability Extreme Events: A KL-Regularized Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Planning Method
summary: The increasing penetration of renewable energy makes power systems more vulnerable to low-probability extreme events, elevating system planning to a critical role in ensuring reliability. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) based on the Wasserstein distance is widely used to address this challenge. However, we find that the conventional Wasserstein ambiguity set tends to excessively amplify the probabilities of low-probability extreme events, leading to over-conservative investment decisions. To mitigate this over-conservatism, this paper proposes a novel ambiguity set that modifies the Wasserstein distance with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term. By leveraging the KL divergence's sensitivity to relative probability changes, the proposed set effectively curbs the unrealistic magnification of low-probability events. A two-stage distributionally robust planning model built upon this new ambiguity set is developed to optimize the installed capacity of photovoltaic, wind, and energy storage. The complex model is then reformulated as an equivalent exponential cone program with strict theoretical proofs, making it computationally tractable. Numerical results on the PJM 5-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems reveal the over-conservatism of standard Wasserstein DRO under low-probability extreme events and validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed planning model and solution algorithm.

title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
summary: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.

title: From Transfer Probes to Expert Grouping: Evidence from LoRA Post-Training
comment: Technical report for training resources allocation for specialization of LLMs
summary: A platform that post-trains one base model for many business lines often has more lines than experts it can maintain, so lines must share experts, yet lines seldom come with a taxonomy saying which should share. We ask whether transfer probes (train on one source, measure paired changes on all sources) can discover a grouping when the standard one is unknown. To test probes against a reference, we use seven public sources that do have a label tree (five mathematics subfields and two kinds of programming, standing in for business lines) and treat the tree's grouping as a label reference that the evaluator holds and the method does not. With four LoRA experts under fixed per-source exposure and per-expert budgets, we compare a purely probe-derived grouping and an uninformed uniform default (whose tied routing serves every line from one expert) against this reference. Trained once for one interval from a shared warm-up state and routed by a rule fixed by each allocation, neither reached the prespecified practical gain of 2 percentage points, and both had lower overall utility than the reference ($-2.43$ and $-2.54$ pp; 95\% intervals below zero). In a post hoc comparison, the probe-derived grouping was indistinguishable from the uniform default ($+0.11$ pp, $[-1.25,+1.54]$). In fixed-budget LoRA post-training, a grouping built from initial-state single-source probes thus did not deliver the advantage predicted from the probes once carried to a later training state, a finite budget, and specified routing.

title: When Does Compensating Inherited Quantization Error Help? Mean-Square Guarantees for Layer-Wise Quantization and Their Limits
summary: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.

title: Deterministic Distributed Linearly Separable Computation via Nested Cyclic Codes
summary: We study the $(K,N,S,M,K_c)$ distributed linearly separable computation (DLSC) setting, where a master employs $N$ workers with a per-worker computation load of $M$ to recover $K_c$ deterministic linear combinations of $K$ messages in the presence of up to $S$ stragglers. We propose a DLSC framework based on nested cyclic codes that achieves $M=\frac{K}{N}(S+K_c)$. For sufficiently large $K$, we establish the matching converse $M\geq\frac{K}{N}(S+K_c)$, proving the asymptotic computation load optimality of the proposed framework. By instantiating cyclic locally recoverable codes (LRCs) as base codes in the framework, the master can recover the desired $K_c$ linear combinations by contacting fewer than $N-S$ workers under many straggler scenarios. This essentially softens the straggler threshold without increasing the computation load or communication cost. Finally, we extend the construction to reduce the per-worker communication load by a factor of $m$, while achieving an asymptotically optimal computation load of $M=\frac{K}{N}(S+mK_c)$.

title: Infrastructure-Aware Runtime Protection of Co-Deployed AI Services at the Industrial Edge
summary:
In modern production lines, a single edge device simultaneously runs multiple AI services like a torque-control model, a vision inspector, a predictive maintenance routine. All these services run on the same CPU and same shared network segment. When the shared network segment saturates, the services do not crash. The services just produce outputs that are inaccurate or stale, and no longer reflect the plant's conditions. Our paper targets this class of silent, partial failure scenarios in Industrial Edge Systems.
  We treat each co-deployed service as an autonomous agent. We introduce the Runtime Criticality Score (RCS), which each service agent uses to express at any moment, its intrinsic utility and survival urgency under resource constraints. The score is computed from six normalized dimensions covering physical consequence, inference quality, input freshness, recent availability stress, actuator coupling, and available protective actions on the host. Its dimension weights are adjusted online through a lightweight Bayesian update driven by the type of disturbance currently observed, so the same service is ranked differently under a network delay than under thermal throttling. Agents publish their RCS to peers over an open, peer-to-peer discovery channel, and use it to negotiate three things without a central controller: (i) local threshold enforcement on their own host, (ii) migration to a willing peer when the current host can no longer protect them, (iii) reassignment of the coordination role when the incumbent coordinator is itself impaired. Beyond the immediate benefit of catching silent degradation, the framework contributes a concrete instance of decentralized, physically grounded agent coordination. Agents belonging to different owners can advertise capabilities, bid for protection, and reorganize across an open network.

title: CircuitBreak: Pruning a Sparse Safety Circuit of Neurons
summary: White-box neuron pruning has shown that refusal in large language models (LLMs) can depend on a small, removable set of feed-forward (FFN) channels. Existing attacks either need carefully paired ``twin'' prompts or score each neuron in isolation. Pruning also has an unavoidable capability cost, so over-removal compounds the loss. TwinBreak removes $1\%$--$5\%$ of parameters and NeuroStrike removes $0.3\%$--$0.7\%$ of neurons in targeted layers. We model safety as a small \emph{circuit} whose neurons contribute jointly rather than independently. We propose \textsc{CircuitBreak}, a neuron-pruning attack that greedily searches for a sparse set of FFN neurons whose joint ablation flips a refusal readout. \textsc{CircuitBreak} re-scores every candidate after the neurons already removed and needs no twin prompts. On ten instruction-tuned models, the greedy search converges after removing $29$--$150$ neurons ($0.0066\%$--$0.0388\%$ of the MLP). The pruned models raise the attack success rate from $2.24\%$/$7.35\%$ to $87.54\%$/$87.54\%$ on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from $8.95\%$/$5.43\%$ to $88.50\%$/$88.18\%$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, as judged by Llama Guard 3 8B on StrongREJECT.

title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $ρ$ by $ρ^α$ for a data-adaptive exponent $α\in[0,1]$: $α=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $α=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $α$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $κ$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$α$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.

title: Delay-Doppler Duality: Simplifying Exact Equalization of Zak-OTFS in Time or in Frequency
summary: The Zak-OTFS carrier waveform is a pulse in the delay-Doppler (DD) domain, and given the input-output (I/O) relation at one DD point in a frame, we can predict the I/O relation at all other points. While it is simple to acquire the effective wireless channel with Zak-OTFS, the cost of embracing inter-carrier interference is equalization complexity. The cost of linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) equalization grows cubically with the frame size. We describe how to use channel knowledge to reduce equalization complexity. For any pulse shaping filter, and for fractional delays and Dopplers, we show that the DD channel matrix is unitarily similar, through the discrete Zak transform, to a time-domain (TD) matrix that is a weighted sum of cyclic delay and Doppler operators, where the weights are the taps of the effective channel. We also obtain a dual frequency-domain (FD) form through an additional Fourier transform. The TD matrix is banded with a width set by the delay spread that is independent of the Doppler spread, whereas the FD matrix is banded with a width set only by the Doppler spread. We design a receiver that reads off the two widths from the channel estimate, selects the cheaper domain, and solves the banded system exactly, using a bordered Cholesky factorization that treats the quasi-periodic wrap-around without sacrificing degrees of freedom. Filters that decay slowly need a few preconditioned conjugate gradient steps. We show that the complexity of equalization becomes linear in the frame size. Simulations match direct DD-LMMSE error rates with three to four orders of magnitude fewer multiplications. A single receiver handles channels with very different delay and Doppler characteristics.

title: Full classification of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard codes
summary: The $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive codes are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}^n$. A $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard (GH) code is a GH code over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ which is the Gray map image of a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive code. A recursive construction gives such codes $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$, of type $(n;t_1,\dots,t_s)$ and length $p^t$, and a partial classification of them is known. In this paper, we complete the classification of these codes for every prime $p$. The main tool is the derived code, obtained by puncturing the code outside a block of coordinates determined by its kernel. For a nonlinear code $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$ with $t_1\geq2$, the derived code is a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{s-1}}$-linear GH code of the same family, although the mechanism for odd $p$ differs from the binary one. As a consequence, for $t\geq3$, there are $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)$ nonequivalent such codes of length $p^t$ if $p$ is odd, and $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)-1$ if $p=2$, where $\mathcal P(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$. In particular, this completes the classification of the $\mathbb{Z}_{2^s}$-linear Hadamard codes. We also prove a conjecture on the codes with $t_1\geq2$ and $t_s=0$.

title: Adaptive Handling of Deadline Misses via Stochastic MPC
summary: Real-time control systems may experience sporadic computational overloads that cause controller executions to overrun their expected deadlines, affecting the timely update of control inputs. Such overruns are classically handled with static decisions, e.g., by either stopping and discarding the late execution at the deadline instant, or continuing it while skipping the next activations. This paper first demonstrates that such static policies can lead to suboptimal performance when the controlled system undergoes varying operating conditions, and thus proposes a control-driven hybrid overrun strategy that optimally adapts the deadline miss handling at runtime. We model the closed loop as a Markov jump linear system, whose modes encode overrun histories, and we formulate a scenario-tree-based stochastic model predictive control problem that predicts and optimizes over possible sequences of deadline hits and misses. We evaluate our proposal on linear benchmarks including a double integrator and an aircraft pitch system.

title: CT0: Cybersecurity Transformer
summary: General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and CT0-Micro, its first incarnation: a compact (~4B-parameter) model built on the open base model, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: CT0-Micro solves 21.1% of cybench-subtask against 7.6% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: CT0-Micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5% accuracy in 47 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5% in 254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.966 in 8 ms, and, generating only for the facts it is unsure about, extracts vulnerability facts more accurately than either mode alone at a fifth of the generative cost. All of it is built in about 314 RTX PRO 6000 GPU-hours and served from one workstation GPU, with no policy layer between operator and target. Across eighteen benchmarks and use cases run with one checkpoint and head, we report where the design helps, where it does not, and what it still lacks.

title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
summary: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

title: Robust Quickest Change Detection with Cost-Efficient Experiment Design and Unknown Post-Change Model
summary: A quickest change detection problem is studied where the decision-maker has access to multiple experiments, but can choose only one experiment at a time to detect the change. The true post-change distribution under each experiment is unknown, but known to belong to a family of distributions. It is assumed that each of these families of distributions has an element that is least favorable in a well-defined sense. An algorithm is proposed that is designed using the least favorable distributions. It is shown that the algorithm is first-order asymptotically optimal, as the rate of false alarms goes to zero. This algorithm minimizes the worst-case average detection delay over all post-change distributions within the assumed families, subject to a constraint on the average run length to false alarm and constraints on the average fraction of time each experiment is performed before change.

title: Rate-Splitting Multiple Access for RIS-Enabled Full-Duplex Communications with User Relaying
summary: Rate splitting multiple access (RSMA) has emerged as a promising non-orthogonal transmission mechanism to improve spectral- and energy efficiency, and user fairness in multi-antenna broadband channels. To further enhance its performance, in this paper we investigate a novel cooperative RSMA (C-RSMA) transmission framework assisted by reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) and user relaying. More specifically, we first formulate the common- and private-rate maximization problem satisfying the transmit power constraint, by jointly optimizing the transmit beamformers at the BS and the reflective beamformer at the RIS. The above formulated problem is an intractable and NP-hard problem as the optimization variables are coupled and the strong residual self-interference (SI) is involved. To conquer the challenge mentioned above, we propose a low-complexity alternative optimization approach to jointly optimize the transmit and reflective beamforming. Simulation results show that our approach is capable of enabling superior sum-rate performance than the RIS-assisted space division multiple access (SDMA), half-duplex RSMA, and SDMA without using RIS schemes.

title: Computation of Price Signals for Controlling Flexible Prosumers in Distribution Grids Incorporating Stochasticity and Fairness
summary: This paper proposes a method for distribution system operators (DSOs) to design spatially fair dynamic price signals for flexible prosumers, accounting for both distribution grid constraints and the stochastic behavior of prosumers. Since locational pricing can introduce price unfairness when grid constraints are active, the proposed approach includes mechanisms to enforce price fairness across the network. The method involves the DSO solving a scenario-based optimal power flow (OPF) problem to derive, similarly to locational marginal prices in transmission systems, the Lagrange multipliers associated with grid constraints and to compute individualized price signals for each prosumer under various PV generation and demand scenarios. Subsequently, two methods are introduced to aggregate these individualized prices into a single fair price across prosumers. Their performance is evaluated through simulations on a model distribution grid, comparing prosumer revenues, grid constraint violations, and analyzing the impact of fairness on reducing cost variance among prosumers.

title: PrivacyGuard: Source-Linked Sanitization and Locally Resolvable PII References for Cloud GUI Agents
summary: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII). Existing placeholder defenses mask detected spans and reuse exact strings. Fragmented or changed forms can expose PII or break entity continuity across turns. PrivacyGuard addresses this private reference problem with source-linked sanitization (SAN) and a structured reference lifecycle (REF). SAN reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent. REF links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, PrivacyGuard reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55\%--82.60\% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system in all four reader--language combinations. REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 under exact-value reuse to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks, verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30. On AndroidLab, PrivacyGuard achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success point estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners. On PrivScreen, it reduces fixed-reader field exposure by 62.72\%--62.84\% relative to the same baseline. PrivacyGuard lowers upload exposure while preserving a locally resolvable task path.

title: Learning to Extrapolate in Depth with Looped Transformers
summary: Looped transformers reuse a single block across iterations, raising a natural question: how far can a block trained at one depth be safely extrapolated to greater depths? We study this question for all-pairs graph connectivity, where harder graphs require longer-range information propagation. We show that under exchangeability and symmetric positive initialization, population training at depth K converges to an update rule governed by a single effective parameter that balances graph propagation against fitting structure unresolved at training depth. This trade-off creates a finite extrapolation window: too few test-time loops provide insufficient propagation, while too many eventually create false connections. We derive explicit endpoints for this window and bound the graph hardness solvable beyond training as a function of training depth and hardness. In particular, a test depth chosen solely from the training distribution can guarantee recovery on substantially harder graphs, with a certified depth gain that grows exponentially as training depth outpaces training hardness. Experiments validate the predicted windows and show how compute budget and initialization affect the optimal training depth.

title: Universal Distributed Feature Extraction Complementary to Side Information via H-Score
summary: This paper considers a distributed estimation system where edge nodes transmit averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation. A key challenge arises when the center node possesses auxiliary side information: how to design local extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task, while avoiding redundancy with the side information. To tackle this problem, we orthogonally decompose the joint function space and demonstrate in the weak-dependence regime that the modal decomposition of the canonical dependence kernel's conditional-additive component yields optimal, task-independent features. We construct a distributed nested H-score to learn this decomposition and show that, under a limited feature budget, the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes, and vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.

title: Solomonoff induction of selected bits and online classification
summary:
Solomonoff induction is a general solution for sequence prediction that started the field of algorithmic information theory around 1960. Let $M$ be the universal semimeasure. After observing a string $ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1}$, it predicts the next bit $ω_n$ to be $b$ with conditional probability proportional to $M(ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1} b)$. Thus the error of this probability is \[
  e_ω(n) = 1 - \frac {M(ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1}ω_n)} {M(ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1} 0) + M(ω_{1} \cdots ω_{n-1} 1)}. \] If $ω$ a computable infinite sequence with a self-delimiting description of at most $k$ bits, then $\sum_n e_ω(n) \le k\ln 2+O(1)$. Lattimore, Hutter and Gavane consider the problem of predicting computable patterns in a sequence, for example, the pattern of repeated bits $ω= 00\,11\,00\,00\,11\,00\cdots$ They show that the error probabilities of the bits fixed by a computable pattern have limit zero, for example, for repeated bits, one has $\lim_n e_ω(2n) = 0$. We show that for some computable pattern, the sum of $e_ω(n)$ over positions $n$ from the pattern is not bounded. However, the sum of squares $(e_ω(n))^2$ is bounded exponentially in the program length of the pattern. It is also shown that bits of $ω$ that are fixed by a computable classification function $f:\{0,1\}^* \rightarrow \{0,1\}$, converges faster: the sum of $(e_ω(n))^2$ is bounded by a polynomial in the program length for programs whose runtime is bounded by any fixed computable time bound.

title: Impact of Data Center Load on Co-Optimized Generation and Transmission Expansion Planning with Embedded Unit Commitment
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC)
summary: The rapid growth of hyperscale data centers challenges grid expansion planning, yet existing studies focus largely on operational flexibility rather than long-term investment decisions. This paper examines how large data center loads sited at multiple buses affect co-optimized Transmission Expansion Planning (TEP) and Generation Expansion Planning (GEP). The problem is formulated as a multi-year, Unit Commitment (UC)-embedded mixed-integer linear program on the modified IEEE 24-bus Reliability Test System (RTS-24) with Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT)-calibrated renewable energy profiles. A 500 MW data center load, about 17.5% of the base-year peak, is allocated across four buses by voltage level, generation headroom, renewable co-location, and network connectivity. Integrating this load raises the 15-year net present value of total system cost by 1,794 million USD (+61.6%) and the system-average locational marginal price (LMP) by 45.2%, with operating cost dominating capital investment (84.2% versus 15.8%). Renewable curtailment remains negligible: existing renewables are already near full utilization, so the added demand is served almost entirely by incremental thermal generation. Most notably, the load shifts the optimal plan from transmission-only to generation-only, replacing the base-case 230 kV reinforcement with a new 400 MW combined-cycle gas turbine and showing that strategically sited generation can substitute for network reinforcement.

title: Logit Leakage through Floating-Point Bias Addition
summary: Language model APIs can expose token-specific biases while withholding logits and token probabilities. Existing bias-based extraction recovers relative logits, leaving a common additive component undetermined in ideal arithmetic. We identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition that exposes information about this component through token identities alone. The channel distinguishes score vectors with identical complete unperturbed log probabilities. Our method exploits changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries. Under the stated binary32 arithmetic assumptions and a known reachable score interval, it recovers a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries. Given complete relative logits, one recovered anchor determines the original logit vector. We evaluate recovery across 11 public checkpoints from seven model families and extend the local method with adaptive interval search and anchor selection. In end-to-end experiments with vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 Qwen3-0.6B inputs per system, including 64 held-out inputs. A separate token-only experiment extracts a pretrained small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. We also establish a sufficient condition for suppressing common-shift disclosure by subtracting the maximum before bias addition. In controlled experiments, this mitigation eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants and preserves token decisions under the tested random biases.

title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
summary: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.

title: Making Tensor Decoupling More Robust and Less Parametric
summary: Tensor decoupling algorithms recover compact representations of multivariate functions by combining linear factor matrices with univariate internal nonlinearities. We identify two limitations of recent methods. First, their performance is not invariant to mismatched output or gradient magnitudes, and second, their spline internals require manual tuning of their degrees of freedom. We propose two lightweight fixes. The first is a preprocessing step that rescales the input Jacobian tensor, removing both the bias towards larger magnitude outputs and the ill-conditioning of certain factor updates caused by such a mismatch. The second replaces B-spline internals by penalized splines coupled with generalized cross-validation, making the method less dependent on the user selecting the right number of control points. Finally, we release an efficient open-source JAX implementation of our algorithm.

title: On Han- and Shearer-Type Information Inequalities: Equality Conditions and Combinatorial Applications
summary: Madiman and Tetali established strong and weak fractional inequalities that subsume classical entropy subset inequalities such as Han's inequality and Shearer's lemma. In this work, we derive a decomposition of the gap in the strong fractional inequality and use it to establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for equality in the strong form of Han's inequality. As a consequence, we characterize the equality conditions for a strong Loomis-Whitnet-type projection inequality of Balister and Bollobas (2012). Finally, we apply the weak fractional inequality to an extremal graph theory problem, recovering and extending results of Sason (2022) and Boucheron et al. (2013), whose approaches rely on Han's inequality.

title: Impact of Security Modeling Fidelity on Hyperscale Data Center Hosting Capacity Assessment
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the 2027 IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies Conference & Exposition
summary: This paper assesses hyperscale data center hosting capacity in transmission grids. Hosting capacity (HC) analysis quantifies the maximum additional load a bus can accommodate without violating operational constraints. This paper defines data center HC as the maximum time-invariant active power demand at a single target bus over a 24-hour peak-day horizon, and evaluates it under four models of increasing fidelity (i.e., the extent to which the model enforces real-world operational security requirements) on the modified IEEE 24-bus system: (i) DC optimal power flow (DC-OPF) without unit commitment (UC), (ii) basic SCUC (security-constrained unit commitment) without reliability constraints, (iii) SCUC with spinning reserve, and (iv) N-SCUC with both reserve and branch-contingency security. Comparing these models quantifies the impact of unit commitment, reserve requirements, and N-1 security on bus-level HC estimates. The N-SCUC yields an average HC of 444 MW; omitting N-1 security raises this to 532 MW, a 19.8% overestimation. The DC-OPF and basic SCUC models further overestimate HC, indicating a trade-off between model complexity and estimation accuracy.

title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.

title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
summary:
Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships.
  We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks.
  GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.

title: On the Multi-Weight Shift-Sum Iterative Decoding of Short BCH Codes
summary: This paper investigates a shift-sum decoding algorithm that employs dual codewords. Existing dual codeword shift-sum decoding schemes mainly rely on minimum-weight dual codewords. However, the number of such codewords is often limited, which restricts the amount of reliability information available to the decoder. To address this issue, we extend the component counting mechanism from minimum-weight dual codewords to dual codewords whose Hamming weights lie within a prescribed upper bound. We further introduce a normalized component counting rule to suppress the overcounting bias caused by the much larger populations of higher-weight classes. Based on this framework, we develop a hard-decision iterative error reduction decoder and a soft information-aided iterative error reduction decoder. Numerical results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing minimum-weight shift-sum baselines especially for short codes where additional dual codeword information is particularly valuable.

title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
summary: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.

title: Evidence-Governed Deployment Readiness for Networked Agents on Industrial OT Infrastructure
summary:
Deploying a workload on a cyber-secure industrial operational-technology (OT) network requires many cross-layer prerequisites to hold at once, including persistent addressing, name resolution, time synchronization, certificate trust, proxy traversal, and reachable industrial-protocol endpoints. These are owned by different teams, yet current tools treat pre-deployment checking, fault attribution, remediation, and ongoing compliance as separate problems, so evidence is rarely reused across stages. As edge platforms come to host self-adapting agents on shared infrastructure, this fragmentation becomes a governance problem. All four stages ask one question: do a workload's requirements hold on a given network?
  We present an evidence-governed framework that answers it through a single reference, a versioned network-intent artifact specifying a workload's cross-layer requirements for a specific release. A coverage-driven test loop attaches tested evidence to each requirement before deployment. At a site, readiness is reported as ready, not ready, or undecidable, separating untested requirements from genuine failures; a repair step proposes fixes that preserve co-located workloads; and a drift-watch component re-evaluates the site on change, extending assurance across the workload's lifetime. A multi-workload OPC UA commissioning case illustrates all four stages. By detecting runtime deviations and suspending an agent's guarantees until a refreshed artifact is registered, the framework grounds auditable governance for adapting agent collectives on shared industrial infrastructure.

title: Beyond User-Side Defenses: Image Protection in Open-Weight Diffusion Models
summary: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.

title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.

title: FedLoRD: Personalized Federated Learning based on Low-Rank Structures of Model Parameter Differences
summary: We propose FedLoRD, a personalized federated learning (PFL) method based on the low-rank structure of the differences between the global and personalized model parameters. PFL is a branch of federated learning that aims to learn models tailored to the local data of each client under biased local data distributions. In its local training, each client learns a personalized model by regularizing the difference between its model parameters and the global ones sent from the server. The regularization function needs to be designed with priors on the model parameter difference; however, the existing PFL methods rely on empirical choices (e.g., $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-norms), which do not take into account the actual characteristics of the difference. The resulting mismatch of priors can lead to suboptimal personalized models. To address this issue, we propose a PFL method whose regularizer is built on an observed characteristic of the model parameter differences: they are approximately low-rank at every layer. In our method, we first formulate a local training problem with nuclear norm regularization on the layer-wise differences. We further rewrite this problem via the factorized representation of the nuclear norm so that it can be efficiently solved by a plain stochastic gradient descent method. Image classification experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedLoRD outperforms several existing PFL methods.

title: Optimal Support Size Testing
summary: We present an optimal tester for support size that determines whether an unknown probability distribution is supported on $n$ elements or $\varepsilon$-far away (in total variation distance) with sample complexity $Θ(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)})$, improving the prior best $O(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)} \log(\min\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, n\}))$ due to Ferreira Pinto Jr. and Harms (STOC 2025). As a generalization, we provide a pretty good lower bound on support size.

title: Shadow Pricing in Transient Stability-Constrained Optimal Power Flow
summary: Transient stability constraints alter the economic dispatch of power systems, while the resulting price signals and their implications for market settlement remain insufficiently characterized. Existing approaches identify stability-related components in locational marginal prices, without deriving shadow prices for individual assets, such as generators and loads, or analyzing the resulting settlement. To address this gap, this paper derives shadow prices from a transient stability-constrained optimal power flow in which the differential-algebraic equations governing the system dynamics are embedded through direct discretization. Each shadow price decomposes into a nodal energy component and a stability component, the latter formed by the dual variables of the dynamic equations in which the power of the asset appears. Shadow prices are therefore asset-specific: co-located generators and loads are assigned the same nodal energy component, but can be subject to different stability components when their transient behaviors differ. Case studies on the WECC 9-bus system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system show that settlement at the proposed shadow prices allocates the cost of the stability constraints among the assets without any side payment. An asset that reduces the stability margin is charged its stability component, whereas an asset that improves it is paid, and no generator is dispatched at a loss.

title: Toward Realistic Privacy Risk in FL-Enabled OT Intrusion Detection Systems
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Fast Abstract presented at IEEE QRS 2026 (Florence, Italy)
summary: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.

title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
summary: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.

title: Revisiting Error Feedback for Model Quantization
summary: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.

title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal
summary: A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so ``closer'' can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff's guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff's predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.

title: Rethinking electrified transportation: The case for dynamic wireless charging
summary: Long-term infrastructure investment often requires choosing between an established technology and a capital-intensive alternative that gains value as demand matures. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, this trade-off is between incumbent stationary charging technology and emerging dynamic wireless charging (DWC). DWC could fundamentally alter transportation electrification by enabling high-throughput charging in motion and reducing reliance on large onboard batteries; however, its high upfront cost makes the timing and location of deployment critical. Overcommitting to stationary charging stations (SCS) risks technological lock-in and forgoing the benefits of DWC, whereas premature DWC deployment can strand capital in underutilized corridors. Through a joint investment assessment framework coupling DWC, SCS, and supporting grid infrastructure across nearly 49,000 miles of the US Interstate freight network, we find that higher utilization and longer project lifetimes rapidly shift investment toward DWC, whose share rises sharply from 48% at a project lifetime of 30 years to 100% at 32 years. Contiguous DWC segments can share grid connections, enabling them to provide over six times the rated charging capacity of SCS while requiring 46% less investment in new distribution-grid infrastructure. We also find that a combined DWC and SCS portfolio reaches a maximum lifetime value of USD 60 billion, 63% above the case with only SCS. We further identify specific traffic demand, construction, and grid access conditions that shape where each technology becomes advantageous, yielding actionable thresholds for SCS and DWC deployment that directly inform long-term EV charging infrastructure investment and policy.

title: Security and robustness analysis of encrypted communications for local home automation: ESPHome Native API and MQTT over TLS 1.3
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Systematized review. Submitted to the International Journal of Network Security & Its Applications (IJNSA)
summary: The expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) in residential and local automation environments has highlighted the limitations of considering the internal network as an inherently trusted domain. Man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, such as ARP spoofing, can allow traffic interception or manipulation when communications lack appropriate confidentiality, integrity, and authentication mechanisms. This paper presents a systematized review of the security mechanisms used by two communication alternatives between ESP-family microcontrollers and the Home Assistant platform: MQTT protected through TLS 1.3 and the ESPHome Native API, whose encryption is based on the Noise Protocol Framework using the Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 pattern. The analysis considers four dimensions: cryptographic robustness, attack surface, implementation complexity, and resource consumption. The review identifies significant differences resulting from the architecture and cryptographic model of each alternative. TLS 1.3 provides a standardized framework compatible with public-key infrastructure and formal identity management, though it introduces greater configuration complexity and computational overhead during session establishment. The ESPHome Native API employs a more specialized scheme with lower operational complexity, eliminates dynamic algorithm negotiation, and uses ChaCha20-Poly1305. The resource-consumption analysis relies on measurements published by the projects and manufacturers themselves, not on an experimental test bench, and this limitation is explicitly acknowledged. The results identify the conditions under which each mechanism is appropriate for local home-automation architectures and provide a basis for designing IoT systems that balance security, interoperability, and resource constraints.

title: Query-Adaptive Neuron Steering for LLMs
summary: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.

title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, submitted to the International Journal of Forecasting
summary: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids.
