The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance in magnetic core loss transfer learning.

title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
summary: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.

title: HodgePhaseNet: Discrete Hodge Decomposition of Semantic Flows in Transformer Attention
summary: WavePhaseNet introduced frequency-resolved semantic representations, QuantumPhaseNet introduced gauge-covariant phase connections, and ModularPhaseNet made a finite cyclic phase channel and its cycle holonomy computable in an ordinary Transformer. These constructions are complementary, yet they do not by themselves separate an observed collection of pairwise relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around a larger unfilled cycle. HodgePhaseNet addresses this separation by representing semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex. With vertex-edge incidence matrix $B_1$ and edge-face incidence matrix $B_2$, every such field has a unique orthogonal decomposition $Ω= B_1^TΦ+ B_2Ψ+ H$, where $B_1H=0$ and $B_2^TH=0$. The three component fields are unique even when their potentials are not. We give explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and a redesigned attention interface. The attention bias is defined on allowed ordered query-key pairs, remains consistent under arbitrary choices of edge orientation, and preserves a decoder's causal information boundary by constructing its complex from the visible prefix. Gauge invariance of the attention output is conditional on using invariant or appropriately compensated features. A simple difference of vertex embeddings has no coexact or harmonic component; a genuine relation encoder is therefore indispensable. Local circulation is not automatically contradiction, and harmonic flow is not automatically missing knowledge. These interpretations and any reduction in factual error require controlled empirical evaluation. This paper presents a mathematical and architectural proposal, not external natural-language performance results.

title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
summary: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.

title: Fitting Every Hint Is Not Enough: Premature Floods in Recurrent Algorithmic Reasoners
summary: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and run for many more steps on large ones. On breadth-first search in SALSA-CLRS, we find that a reasoner can reproduce every training hint and still fail on deep graphs: after some exact steps, it declares nodes reached before the search gets there. We call this a premature flood and trace two routes to it. In our GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and set off when that input is in the tail of the training distribution. Setting the input higher at inference brings the flood sooner, and none of the six flooding models counts steps. Without the input, summing the neighbors' states instead of averaging them also breaks the processor. In the benchmark's own GIN and PGN, trained with its code, some seeds instead flood from a fixed step, on sparse and dense graphs alike. Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor. Detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor (0 of 23 seeds, against 6 under full backpropagation) but not with sums or a residual update, and two published remedies leave floods. None of the benchmark's test sets is both deep and dense, but its deepest one shows the second route: on its Delaunay graphs at 1,600 nodes, one GIN seed floods from step 18. We therefore recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.

title: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Testing and Automation of Open RAN Systems: GNG-OTA Framework
comment: This paper has been pubblished in 2025 IEEE International Conference on Omni-layer Intelligent Systems (COINS)
summary: Open Radio Access Networks (O-RAN) empower operators with choice and customization through their disaggregated and interoperable architecture. However, ensuring interoperability in O-RAN presents challenges due to complex testing environments and evolving specifications. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing the Generative AI and Graph Neural Network-based Open RAN Testing and Automation (GNG-OTA) framework. GNG-OTA utilizes state-of-the-art AI techniques including generative AI, natural language processing, and graph neural networks to enable accurate, reliable, efficient, and automatic O-RAN interoperability and performance testing.

title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
comment: 10 pages main body, 56 pages references and appendix, 8 figures. Under review
summary: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing. Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $α$-divergence family.

title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
summary: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network. For each action, the same channel simulator is evaluated under an attack-free and an attacked configuration. Receiver-level residuals are combined with spatial jamming footprints and accumulated to form a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.

title: Characterizing the Separability Gap in Prior-Data Fitted Networks
summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are transformers pretrained on simulated datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions. Standard PFN theory assumes a separable task prior, under which the feature distribution and the mechanism generating labels from features are independent. We show that common PFN priors are non-separable, even in simple settings. Consequently, standard pretraining targets a predictive distribution based on a task posterior updated using both the labeled context and the query features. We characterize its difference from the predictive based on the context posterior alone and show that this difference vanishes under posterior concentration. Under misspecification (i.e., when the true joint distribution lies outside the prior's support), however, prior non-separability can favor better feature fit at the expense of conditional label fit. We illustrate the consequences for feature attribution, Bayesian optimization, and martingale checks of Bayesian behavior. The same dependence also enables PFNs to learn from additional unlabeled observations. We demonstrate this with SemiTabICL, a PFN explicitly pretrained to use these observations, which improves accuracy over a matched supervised baseline. Our findings highlight the need for explicit rules on unlabeled data use in PFN evaluation and establish the dependence between feature and label distributions as a consequential prior design choice.

title: The Right to Be Forgotten under Correlation: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs
summary: We study privacy-preserving algorithms that redact information from a correlated dataset. The goal is to reduce the information leakage about sensitive parts. We analytically characterize the optimal tradeoff between privacy (leakage through correlation) and utility (number of redactions) for local mechanisms and binary Markovian correlations. Our result shows how to decompose the mechanism design problem into a sequence of local mechanism design problems and reveals their sequential relation. The optimal mechanism is the solution to a Finite-Horizon Deterministic Markov Decision Process.

title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.

title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
summary: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

title: Conformal Sequential Decision Making With Cost and Sublinear Policy Regret Guarantees
summary: Automated decision makers, such as AI agents that control robots or network devices, must often satisfy hard cost constraints while maintaining competitive performance. In such settings, a cost measure, such as a safety violation rate, energy consumption, or a distortion level, must stay within a given budget in every episode of operation. Furthermore, a cumulative reward metric, accounting for per-step performance, must stay close to the reward of a meaningful reference policy. We formulate this setup as an episodic sequential decision problem in which the state sequence is arbitrary, and the reward and cost may depend on past actions within the same episode. We propose the online conformal episodic agent (OCEA), a policy that selects one candidate action per episode using a regret-controlled algorithm, and switches to a zero-cost action when the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. We prove that OCEA satisfies per-episode cost constraints for every state sequence and for every realization of its internal randomness, while achieving a sublinear expected policy regret with respect to the best action sequence in hindsight from a comparator class satisfying the same per-episode cost constraints. We apply OCEA to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.

title: COMPASS: Membership Inference Attack Against Vision Large Language Models via Adaptive Noise Calibration
summary: Vision large language models (VLLMs) are deployed in privacy-sensitive domains, raising training-data exposure concerns. Existing gray-box membership inference attacks (MIAs) commonly rely on entropy statistics or generated descriptions, requiring costly generation with limited membership separation. Perturbation-based methods instead measure response changes but focus on large perturbations, leaving VLLM membership behavior under smaller perturbations poorly understood. We systematically characterize VLLM membership behavior under controlled Gaussian perturbations across noise levels at fine resolution. We find that optimal perturbation magnitude and membership-signal direction vary across model-dataset pairs. In many settings, a previously unstudied low-noise regime yields stronger separation than large perturbations, with members exhibiting lower divergence than non-members, reversing the conventional score direction. Other settings retain the conventional direction, demonstrating that neither a fixed perturbation magnitude nor a predetermined score orientation is universally reliable. We propose COMPASS, an adaptive gray-box MIA that calibrates both the perturbation magnitude and membership-score direction using a loosely distribution-matched, known non-member reference set. We instantiate COMPASS using Renyi-normalized KL divergence and Renyi divergence, with max-k aggregation over the most informative image-logit positions. Across LLaVA v1.5-7B, MiniGPT-4, and HuluMed-32B, spanning pretraining, instruction-tuning, and medical-image datasets, COMPASS outperforms baselines. On general-domain data, COMPASS achieves AUCs up to 0.88. On the distribution-matched medical evaluation, it reaches 0.64 AUC, while the strongest baseline remains at chance level. These results establish full-range adaptive perturbation analysis as an effective approach to VLLM membership inference.

title: Algorithmic Fairness Over Time: Advances & Prospects
summary: In the presence of feedback loops, algorithmic decisions at one time step can influence observed data in subsequent steps, potentially introducing selection bias or shifts in data distribution. Research has demonstrated that ignoring these effects can lead to unfairness, which may worsen over time as the model remains deployed within society. This raises important questions of how to measure and ensure fairness of algorithmic decision-making models over time. In this short paper, we present a taxonomy that distinguishes between different types of static and temporal fairness notions in recent advancements. We then suggest prospects for future research by identifying common implicit temporal assumptions, open questions to enhance our temporal understanding of fairness, and other open challenges.

title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
summary: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

title: PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Generator-Aware Baselines for Synthetic Node Classification
summary: PATTERN, a synthetic node-classification benchmark still used to rank graph networks, plants a random subgraph in a random host graph and asks which nodes belong to it. Its generator draws 100 patterns once and plants the same ones in every split, so each test graph carries a pattern that also appears in 100 training graphs. A matcher that reads these patterns off the training labels and looks them up in each test graph reaches 99.2 class-weighted accuracy with no trained parameters, against 89.8 for the best published model. Inference under the generator without the patterns reaches 86.8. Two published models, CKGConv and GRIT, score lower on patterns they have not seen: on new graphs with fresh patterns both fall below this pattern-blind predictor, and withholding patterns from CKGConv's training lowers its accuracy on the test graphs that carry them. Training CKGConv with a new pattern in every graph raises its accuracy on fresh patterns by about 2 points, to the level of the pattern-blind predictor, at some cost on the reused patterns. The same kind of inference under the generator matches the best published result on CLUSTER and, without any training, scores above every published result we found on Minesweeper's released board. We recommend that synthetic benchmarks report scores on fresh templates beside reused ones, publish baselines built from their generators, and state how their metric is weighted and pooled.

title: The Maximum Nonlinearity of 8-variable Balanced Boolean Functions is 116
summary: Does there exist an 8-variable balanced Boolean function with nonlinearity 118? This is a famous and long-standing open problem in Boolean functions. In this paper, we give a negative answer to this open problem, and prove that the maximum nonlinearity of balanced Boolean functions in 8 variables is 116, establishing the 8-variable instance of Dobbertin's conjectured recursion for the minimum Walsh peak of balanced functions. Equivalently, the covering radius of the Reed--Muller code RM(1,8) in 0-resilient Boolean functions is 116. We deduce the result by obtaining a quadratic form of polar rank 6, and reducing the problem to the existence of a 6-variable Boolean function with nonlinearity greater than 26 whose Hamming distance to a bent function is between 4 and 6.

title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
summary: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.

title: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
summary:
HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time.
  In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift.
  We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.

title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_Δ$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
summary: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.

title: Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling
summary: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $Ω(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.

title: The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature
summary: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{ηV}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.

title: Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Physical World AI (PhysWorldAI). 15 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables
summary: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. We present a proof of concept toward a multimodal foundation model for plasma state reconstruction during magnetic reconnection, motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE). Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta $β_{e0}=0.2$, with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.

title: On the Theoretical Limits of Learning Unconstrained Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) accelerate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by learning the energies and forces that govern atomic motion. Recent work has shown that relaxing physical inductive biases can improve computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, raising the question of whether energy-and-force matching alone is sufficient to ensure accurate sampling. We show that, for unconstrained hypothesis classes, the relationship between prediction error and sampling accuracy is exponentially ill-conditioned in dimension. In particular, prediction errors that decay exponentially with dimension can coexist with nearly maximal total variation distance between the learned and target distributions. We identify two failure mechanisms. The first is kinetic trapping, where relaxation to an accurate learned equilibrium requires exponentially long times, even when simulations are initialized from training configurations at which energies and forces are matched exactly. The second is equilibrium mismatch, where the learned stationary distribution itself remains far from the target. Under explicit assumptions, we show that equilibrium mismatch can persist even in local, symmetry-preserving models, where small per-atom errors coexist with a distributional discrepancy that approaches its maximum as system size increases. Finally, we establish global energy-control conditions that guarantee equilibrium accuracy and identify additional conditions required for rapid relaxation.

title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
summary: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.

title: Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.

title: Random Feature Pruning for Multi-Class Classification
summary: Weighted sums of random kitchen sinks (W-RKS) is a commonly used feature extraction technique for supervised learning tasks. A major drawback of this method is the redundancy and ineffectiveness of many extracted random features. This paper investigates efficient methods for reducing such redundancy in multi-class classification problems. We specifically formulate feature selection as a variant of the sequentially nested model selection problem and introduce the Successive Empirical Excess Risk Difference Maximization (SEED-MAX) algorithm. It recursively computes empirical risks to identify the most parsimonious yet informative set of features. We derive an analytical lower bound for the probability of correct feature selection by the SEED-MAX algorithm. This lower bound on the probability of correct feature selection can be made arbitrarily close to one by increasing the training dataset size. To further enhance the rate of pruning, we evaluate the features retained by SEED-MAX using the Fisher test (F-Test). Empirical evaluations on UCR time-series classification datasets show that the sequential application of SEED-MAX with the Fisher test achieves approximately 92 percent rate of pruning with negligible degradation in classification accuracy. Implementations of the SEED-MAX and SEED-MAX-F-Test methods are available at https://github.com/OmidiAmin/seed-max-ftest.

title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 MLxOR workshop. Paper contains 6 pages (4 main text, 1 references, 1 appendix); 1 figure and 3 tables
summary: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.

title: scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data
summary: To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder-classifier configurations on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP-derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF-related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro-F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro-F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell-type and disease-state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e-3 and p=4.8e-6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP-derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway-enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state-space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi-task prediction and hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation. Code: https://github.com/UgoLomoio/scHFBiMamba.

title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
summary: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.

title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
summary: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long-Context Foundation Models (non-archival). Extended version: adds a cross-architecture containment comparison on Mamba-2 and corrects two claims in the workshop version. Code and project page: https://avalon-s.github.io/dynamic-scaling-fails/
summary: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.

title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
comment: Accepted to AXIOM: Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning (NeurIPS 2026 workshop). 4 pages + appendix, 4 figures, 5 tables
summary: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.

title: Sensor-Aware Joint Data Fusion and State Estimation under Sparse Multi-rate Distribution Grid Sensing
summary: Distribution-system state estimation is a growing necessity for the modern power grid as the addition of local storage and generation add system complexity that an operator or aggregator is not able to directly monitor. Classical methods work well when all system elements are time-synchronized and at least partly observable, but multi-rate monitoring of sparse heterogeneous sensors typically relies on machine learning approaches. It is a common practice in the literature to structure this task as a two-stage pipeline, first fusing data from disparate sensors and then feeding the fused pseudo-measurements to a separately trained state estimator. We propose a heterogeneous latent graph ODE in which measurement functions and sampling processes are typed and localized on specific buses, paired with a graph- transformer state estimator solving DSSE specifically for multi-rate heterogeneous sensor placements, and demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple IEEE standard topologies as observability degrades.

title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
summary: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion

title: LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications
summary: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.

title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
summary: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
summary: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.

title: DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time
summary: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $ΔS_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.

title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundations of Language Model Security (FLMSec). 10 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

title: Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning of LLMs in Learnable Low-Rank Subspaces
summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.

title: EvolvAttack: Backdooring self Evolving VLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving mechanisms let vision-language model (VLM) agents continually adapt through evolving memory, but they also allow malicious behavior to emerge only after deployment. We introduce a new attack surface, the self-evolving backdoor, whose payload stays dormant in the initial agent and is progressively activated as the agent evolves. Unlike conventional backdoors, which can be exposed by testing triggered inputs on a static model, our attack requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state; static scanning with clean memory thus yields near-zero attack success and may deem the agent benign. We realize this through memory-aware backdoor training, which couples trigger activation with the agent's evolving memory while preserving benign behavior unless the trigger co-occurs with payload-related memory. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack preserves normal functionality and stays nearly inactive before evolution (0.5% attack success rate), yet exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions, revealing a stealthy threat unique to self-evolving agents.

title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
summary: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.

title: Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Reconstruction-based detectors for multivariate time series anomaly detection typically learn a single entangled representation of normal behavior and flag anomalies based on reconstruction error. However, real-world anomalies are not only isolated spikes in a single channel but also disruptions in the relationships between channels, where each sensor individually appears normal, but their joint behavior deviates from the norm. Because these models compress both temporal evolution and inter-channel structure into this single space, they lack an explicit mechanism to isolate such inter-channel dependencies from normal temporal dependencies, leading to lower detection rates for cross-channel anomalies. We propose CARMA (Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), which is a reconstruction-based variational autoencoder with two complementary latent spaces: a temporal latent that captures sequential dynamics, and a correlation latent that is trained to reconstruct the window's pairwise Pearson correlations. Both representations are fused in the signal decoder, and anomalies are detected from the reconstruction error. We evaluate CARMA on the TSB-AD-M benchmark suite (17 datasets, 180 series) against 29 baseline methods, and show that it significantly outperforms all of them across multiple threshold-free and range-aware metrics, achieving a VUS-PR of 0.4929. Ablations show that removing the correlation branch degrades performance, that adding a second latent without supervision recovers only part of the gain, and that supervising the correlation latent with an explicit correlation target accounts for the rest and produces a sharper error response at anomalies.

title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.

title: Imperfect Verifiers, Exact Targets: Inference-Time Scaling for Continuous Generation
summary: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling uses additional computation to score intermediate states and steer generation toward better outputs. However, imperfect intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not ensure recovery of the desired reward-tilted distribution. We introduce Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (CS-VGB), an inference-time scaling method for sampling from reward-tilted distributions with continuous generative models through repeated denoising and renoising. With correctly paired denoising and renoising transitions, the stationary distribution of CS-VGB at the clean checkpoint equals the desired reward-tilted target, even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate. Under stated regularity conditions, CS-VGB converges exponentially to the target despite verifier error, and the expected number of updates needed to reach a clean sample grows only linearly with the number of checkpoints. In analytically tractable settings, we empirically demonstrate that CS-VGB recovers the desired reward-tilted distribution despite verifier error, whereas the compared verifier-based sampling methods fail to recover the target under the same verifier errors. We also instantiate the framework with diffusion models and one-step stochastic posterior maps. Across prompt-guided ImageNet generation, facial-attribute generation on CelebA, and multi-robot planning, recurrent CS-VGB search improves reward and task success as inference budgets grow, with image-generation rewards continuing beyond the observed plateaus of denoising-only baselines.

title: FragFlex: Fragment-Based Flexible Molecular Generation for Exploring Vast Chemical Space
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap
summary: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of an astronomically large chemical space. Molecular graph diffusion models offer a promising approach to this task, but many require graph size to be fixed before generation. Although atom-level insertion and deletion can enable flexible-size generation, jointly modeling molecular size, atom types, and bonds while maintaining chemical validity remains challenging. We introduce FragFlex, a flexible-length discrete diffusion model that performs node insertion and deletion at the fragment level. During denoising, FragFlex jointly learns the size, fragment identities, and inter-fragment connectivity of the fragment graph. A neural attachment-site predictor and valence-aware assembler then convert the generated fragment graph into an atom-level molecule. In large-scale experiments generating 10 million molecules, FragFlex achieves near-perfect chemical validity while maintaining high uniqueness, demonstrating a strong balance between the two.

title: WisdomNet: trustable machine learning toward error-free classification
summary: Misclassification is a critical problem in many machine learning applications. Since even the classifier models with high accuracy (e.g., > 95%) still introduce some misclassification error, it may not be possible to rely on the output of a classifier. In this paper, we introduce trustable learning, which prompts the learning model to yield only the true output, thus avoiding misclassifications. Whenever the model cannot decide the output accurately, the learning model should indicate that there could be a misclassification error if it is forced to classify, and hence, it should reject to make a decision or defer it to a human expert. Therefore, we develop a methodology for trustable learning and apply it to artificial neural networks and show that it is possible to develop a classifier with 0% misclassification error. We propose a novel neural network architecture named WisdomNet that could provide zero prediction error by introducing an additional neuron named as conjugate neuron that would indicate whether the network is able to classify the data correctly or not. The WisdomNet architecture can be applied to any previously built model, and we have evaluated WisdomNet with several network architectures such as multilayer perceptron, convolutional neural network, and deep network on different data sets. The results show that the WisdomNet is able to reduce the classification error rate to 0%, while labeling the data is difficult to classify as `reject' at a low percentage of within around 10%.

title: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies
summary: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($τ$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.

title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
summary: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.

title: CIViC: Evidence Gates for Audio-Conditioned Visual Prediction on Proxy Tasks
summary: Removing audio can shift a visual predictor's output without showing whether the task uses the intended audio information. We introduce Conditional Input and Visual Interpretation Checks (CIViC), a four-gate protocol that links an interpretation to an intervention, held-out task comparison, or endpoint control. We demonstrate CIViC on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint SpeakerVid proxy tasks. In the static face-raster test, cross-actor audio replacement meets the registered detection rule with a small effect; on a separate temporal endpoint, constant-audio fits score better than audio-trained fits in four matched seeds. In the synthetic mixture, the condition-augmented fit has higher 1,000-step RMSE than the audio-only fit (0.1807 vs. 0.1707), with the gap shrinking during training. In the SpeakerVid proxy, the five-feature-zero fit (five low-level audio summaries zeroed; identity, dialogue, and condition inputs retained) has lower whole-frame grayscale RMSE than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds, while aligned audio has lower segment-drift error. The results show that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different interpretations across these proxy tasks.

title: Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum: A Fully Unmasked Non-LLM Curriculum for Craftax
comment: 37 pages, 7 figures. All authors contributed equally as first authors
summary: We introduce Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum (AHC), a domain-informed, rule-based training system for Craftax-Full. AHC combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial-state progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded selection, and original-task practice. It uses no LLM inference and keeps all 43 actions available. At 2,005,401,600 PPO rollout transitions, three primary AHC runs obtain native-task return $46.70\pm0.57$ (sample SD), compared with $41.91\pm1.01$ for fresh native PPO-GTrXL with the same student architecture and evaluation protocol. Evaluation uses ten stochastic rollouts on each of 1024 fixed worlds per model. An additional cohort of three AHC runs reaches $46.08\pm1.23$. Two single-component ablations retain similar mean returns, while jointly freezing difficulty and removing inherited progress gives $45.14\pm2.79$. All-67-achievement profiles show that most of the return difference comes from Intermediate achievements, while the deepest-floor achievements remain unsolved. A Skill-Preflight diagnosis with a 14B teacher shows how prerequisite and floor-access constraints restrict practice. AHC and three 14B diagnostic configurations reach aggregate returns near the reported 80B DiCode mean of 45.88 and below the 235B mean of 48.55. These results show that an explicit curriculum without LLM inference can reach returns comparable to those reported for LLM-generated curricula on Craftax-Full, without action masking.

title: Full Waveform Inversion with a Learned Preconditioner
summary: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI.
