summary: Motivated by applications to cognitive radio networks, multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB) have attracted considerable attention in recent years. The asynchronous variant, in which players are active only at a fraction of timesteps, better reflects real-world decentralized networks, where devices are not permanently active. Despite its practical relevance, this setting remains relatively understudied. Existing work on asynchronous MMAB has focused on homogeneous players, who share the same activation probability, a setting in which the optimal centralized allocation can be easily characterized. In contrast, efficiently computing the optimal allocation in the heterogeneous setting, where players have different activation probabilities, has remained an open problem. In this work, we investigate this problem and first establish its NP-hardness. We then turn to the greedy algorithm, which runs in polynomial time, and prove that it achieves a $\frac{1}{e}$-approximation of the optimal allocation. Furthermore, when players are processed in decreasing order of their activation probabilities, the approximation guarantee improves to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$. Overall, our results establish the greedy algorithm as an efficient approximation to the optimal allocation, providing a practical oracle baseline for the design of online algorithms for heterogeneous asynchronous multi-player bandits.

title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
summary: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.

title: Euclidean Distance-Based Flow Matching
summary: Flow Matching has recently become popular as a technique for generative modeling with applications in many domains. In the standard Flow Matching formulation, we interpret the vector field as the solution of a least-squares regression problem, which is known to be sensitive to contamination. Therefore we leverage the viewpoint of robust statistics and replace the squared Euclidean distance with the Euclidean distance as a regression objective. This seemingly minor change strongly affects the properties of Flow Matching. We provide a probabilistic interpretation of the new regression target as a conditional geometric median and use this characterization to study distributional robustness of the Euclidean Distance-based Flow Matching. We analyze the mathematical properties of this changed objective and the effect of a contaminated target distribution on the involved conditional velocity distributions. We discuss the challenge of directly characterizing the distribution that our method induces. In specific contamination settings we show theoretically that our method yields an improvement for severe contamination. Finally, we present numerical experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10 image dataset where a proportion of the samples has been contaminated. Our Euclidean distance-based Flow Matching shows a clear advantage in scenarios of severe contamination of the target distribution.

title: Unbalanced W-Flow: Unbalanced Wasserstein Drifting under Finite-Batch Marginal Fluctuations
summary: Teacher-free one-step generative models such as W-Flow learn directly from distributional objectives, with the Sinkhorn divergence providing the strongest empirical performance among the energies studied in W-Flow. However, Sinkhorn divergence is based on balanced optimal transport, whose exact marginal constraints can induce undesirable transport under finite minibatch fluctuations. We introduce UW-Flow, which replaces the balanced Sinkhorn energy with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence and derives the corresponding Wasserstein velocity. The resulting dynamics retain W-Flow's cross-minus-self structure, recover the balanced limit, and preserve target identifiability under suitable assumptions. We further characterize the finite-batch velocity error of balanced and unbalanced transport by comparing each minibatch field with its population counterpart. Our analysis identifies conditions under which marginal relaxation yields smaller minibatch-to-population velocity error, and shows that for separated matched modes, balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation while the corresponding Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) sensitivity remains controlled by local transport geometry. Controlled experiments on fixed-support and continuous two-mode distributions support these predictions. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100, UW-Flow improves generation under matched training budgets, with the largest gains in unconditional generation and consistent improvements in the class-conditional setting.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped SGD with Linear Decay
summary: In this paper, we study the last-iterate convergence of clipped stochastic gradient descent under heavy-tailed noise. We assume that the stochastic gradients are unbiased and that the noise has a bounded central $p$-th moment, where $1<p\le2$. For smooth convex objectives, a linearly decreasing learning rate gives a high-probability error bound of order $O(LR^2\log(1/δ)/T+σR(\log(1/δ)/T)^{(p-1)/p})$. We further establish last-iterate guarantees for nonsmooth composite objectives and smooth composite objectives with proximal updates. In addition, when a causal adversary replaces at most $q$ gradients, the same clipped update achieves a bound with $\log(1/δ)$ replaced by $\log(1/δ)+q$. The corresponding lower bounds for the clean and corrupted oracle models are also provided.

title: When More Objectives Make Identification Easier: The Role of Preferences and Feedback
summary: Best-arm identification (BAI) aims to identify the optimal arm using as few samples as possible. While most existing work focuses on a single objective, many real-world applications involve multiple criteria, which motivates the study of BAI in multi-objective bandits. Intuitively, multi-objective identification seems harder, since the learner must identify optimal arms in a higher-dimensional reward space; however, the additional objectives also provide richer feedback that can reduce the required exploration. In this paper, we characterize when and why multiple objectives can make BAI easier. For Gaussian bandits, we establish a characteristic-time lower bound for fixed-confidence identification that holds uniformly across preference orders. Through explicit comparisons under Pareto, linear, and lexicographic preferences, we reveal three phenomena: (i) identifying a larger optimal set can require fewer samples than identifying a unique optimum; (ii) the advantage of vector feedback over coordinate feedback depends fundamentally on the preference order; and (iii) multi-objective identification can require fewer samples than even the easiest corresponding single-objective problem. Finally, we propose Order-Aware Track-and-Stop (OATS), an algorithm that is correct at any prescribed confidence level and asymptotically matches the lower bound.

title: Fairness under Prediction Error in Predict-then-Optimize Pipelines
summary: Fairness constraints in predict-then-optimize pipelines are necessarily enforced on predicted outcomes $\hat{y}$, since true outcomes $y$ are unobserved at decision time. We study whether a demographic parity constraint enforced this way continues to hold against $y$, and how the resulting violation scales with prediction error. Using a budget-constrained allocation problem solved as a linear program, we show empirically that the true-outcome fairness gap grows with prediction error $σ$ and saturates, well fit by $c(1 - e^{-σ/τ})$ with $c = 0.1545 \pm 0.0103$ and $τ= 3.9045 \pm 0.3745$; its mean is invariant to sample size while its variance decays at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ rate. We derive a two-part theoretical bound: a closed-form local sensitivity result showing the gap's first-order response to prediction error depends on only two individuals per group, validated against the solver to within three significant figures; and a universal, error-independent ceiling following from the boundedness of the decision variable, confirmed consistent with but looser than the empirical saturation level. On US Census income data, enforcing demographic parity on a trained predictor's output reduces an unconstrained disparity in true income to roughly one-third of its original size, leaving 34.4% $\pm$ 3.3% (California) and 35.7% $\pm$ 1.8% (Texas) of the disparity intact and undetectable from the predictions alone -- consistent not only in mechanism but in approximate magnitude across two states with different demographics and income distributions, and stable across ten independent train/test splits in each. A fairness constraint that appears fully satisfied at decision time can mask a substantial, systematic violation of the outcome it was meant to protect.

title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
summary: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning

title: Deterministic Prediction as Global Velocity: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecast
summary: Accurate uncertainty quantification is critical for many time series forecasting applications, and recent studies have increasingly adopted generative models to capture predictive uncertainty. Existing approaches often combine deterministic forecasting with generative modeling to improve predictive performance. However, their joint training is typically unstable because the deterministic model is embedded within the generative process, resulting in deep computational graphs and changing the probability transport path. In this work, we propose DV-Flow, a unified flow-matching formulation that incorporates the deterministic predictor as a parallel velocity component rather than as the endpoint of the transport path. This design enables stable end-to-end optimization while subsuming several existing formulations as special cases, allowing direct comparisons among them. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that DV-Flow consistently improves probabilistic forecasting performance over strong baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/tufts-ml/dv-flow-time-series.

title: Geometric Calibration of Supervised Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.

title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
summary: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.

title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing
summary: Message passing neural networks have shown remarkable performance in algorithmic and constraint reasoning, due to their ability to encode the structure of the task directly in the architecture. Recent work has shown that better results can be achieved using recursive transformers trained with deep supervision and truncated recursions, which make extremely deep loops stable to train, and equipped with test-time procedures such as discrete deduction lattices. In this work, we apply the same procedures to message passing networks, and show that the two ingredients are complementary, and lead to parameter efficient models: we obtain about $99\%$ test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a model of $16$k parameters that trains in about $10$ minutes on an H100, or in $9$ hours on a CPU. We further show that the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information needs to cross the graph, making the choice of wiring a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. We conclude by showing that our models transfer zero-shot to larger instances than those seen during training, outperforming popular neural baselines on N-queens and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.

title: Does Pretraining Teach Chemical Language Models Chemistry?
summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pretrained on large corpora of molecules with the aim of learning representations that transfer to diverse downstream tasks. Here, we systematically study the effects of pretraining using a series of such CLMs across 64 molecular property prediction datasets. We find that the downstream gains of pretraining in CLMs do not scale and performance saturates below gradient-boosting baselines. Across the regimes evaluated, only supervised pretraining on traditional physico-chemical descriptors consistently improves downstream performance for the CLMs tested whereas some forms of pretraining result in models worse than a randomly initialized encoder. While models can resolve molecular structure well, they do so no better than a randomly initialized model, suggesting that, at best, CLMs learn descriptor-like properties in addition to low-level token statistics during pretraining, but surprisingly little chemistry beyond what classical molecular features already capture.

title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
summary: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

title: Bayesian Test-Time Inference of Task-Aligned Similarity from Weak Interactive Feedback
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages main text, 25 pages total including appendix; 4 figures, 15 tables
summary: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. We introduce BASIS (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals), a training-free Bayesian method that uses weak test-time feedback to infer which criterion in a supplied, task-specific library governs the current decision. It maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and selects probes by expected information gain. In a finite noisy model, we characterize when the target-criterion pair is recoverable and show why fixed-criterion and fixed-mixture rules can fail under criterion shift. Across concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement, BASIS improves six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%, reasoning accuracy from 72.3% to 73.1%, and refinement win rate from 61.4% to 63.8% over tuned static mixtures. It also exceeds compute-matched best-of-N selection on reasoning (72.1%) and refinement (61.2%). Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and matched controls indicate that adaptive criterion weighting explains much of the benefit, with joint target-criterion inference adding further value. BASIS selects only among supplied criteria and does not discover new ones.

title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
summary: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
summary: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

title: A Refresh Interval Does Not Fully Specify a Refresh Schedule: Learning-Rate-Dependent Placement in Kronecker-Preconditioned Language Model Training
summary: Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers recompute a cached curvature eigendecomposition only periodically, and implementations and adaptive methods control this through the refresh frequency. We show that frequency leaves part of a schedule free: at a fixed number of refreshes, when they occur changes held-out loss at the same compute. Training GPT-style models with the Mousse optimizer across model sizes, we move the middle refreshes of a four-refresh schedule while fixing the first and last. On FineWeb the two placements exchanged rank as the learning rate rose (later placement was better at low rates, earlier placement at high ones), so a single-learning-rate comparison can report either ranking. The reversal held under controls including the published optimizer internals, and placement still mattered at the published refresh density. The learning rate at which the preference flips fell with model size, consistent with a held-out smaller model, and shifted with training length. A spectral-width staleness score predicted the same ranking at every learning rate and missed the reversal. Refresh schedules should be reported in full and compared across the learning rates at which they will be used.

title: Learning Source Structure: Bayesian Prediction with Transformers
comment: 45 pages, 12 figures. 9 pages of main text. Code at https://github.com/urbanke/learning-source-structure
summary: A transformer trained on sequences whose source parameters are drawn afresh each time can learn only what the sequences share: the source family and its prior. The Bayesian predictor that knows both, which we call informed Bayes, is the unique minimizer of the training loss and is computable from the family alone; we use it as a quantitative, falsifiable reference. Where earlier work compared transformers with Bayes on sources whose contexts can be learned independently, we build Markov sources with up to 64 symbols in which observations in one context inform prediction in another: product sources with known or hidden encodings, transition rows sharing an unknown base law and depth, and a mixture of three families. Our main result is that informed Bayes predicts, from the family and prior alone, how a trained transformer behaves in four tests that go beyond the learning curve: the loss that remains under a source outside the training family (predicted 2.237 bits, measured 2.309), the doubling of the extra loss when two independent components change rather than one (0.345 predicted, 0.350 measured), the benefit of other contexts when a token appears for the first time, and the depth at which copying an earlier continuation starts to pay. On the learning curves themselves, small transformers match informed Bayes when the shared structure is visible in the tokens, and hidden structure needs more layers and training, with gaps below 0.01 bits per token for the largest models. We explain why the imitation is possible and where it must fail: informed Bayes decomposes into sufficient statistics that attention selects and accumulates and an estimator, fixed by the prior, that the feed-forward network learns; training pays the complexity of informed Bayes under the architecture's prior, and finite-memory universal prediction bounds how closely a bounded network can reach it.

title: On the Monitorability of Natural Language Autoencoders: Identification vs Discrimination
summary: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) are proposed as oversight tools for language models: an Activation Verbaliser (AV) writes an English explanation of an activation vector, and an Activation Reconstructor (AR) maps the explanation back to a vector. Their value for oversight depends on a human monitor being able to tell a true account of an activation from a false one, given the Av's explanation. We formalise NLA training and NLA oversight deployment as two different referential games from Emergent Communication: training is a generative referential game, while oversight is a discriminative, multi-modal, partially-observable referential game played over a many-to-many relation between the monitored language model's activations and the accounts that are true of them. The gap between the two games predicts that AV's explanations will identify which activation they describe without discriminating its true account from closely matched false ones, since training never asks explanations to rule anything out. Using the NLA's own AR as a maximally-sympathetic surrogate monitor model, we experimentally confirm this theoretical insight on one released checkpoint: true accounts beat accounts of other activations in all 320 comparisons, but beat fluent rivals differing in a single claim only 60.2% of the time (std.err. 6.7%, chance at 50%, $n = 35$). A meaning-preserving rewrite by an uninvolved model costs only 2.1% of the distance to another activation's account, so the failure is not due to the NLA pair having developed private conventions in the AV's explanations. Our rival accounts test only transcript-level truths, which the monitored language model's conversation settles, so these results bound the easiest case and leave claims about the monitored model's own processing untested. We state conjectures that would make both results consequences of the framework.

title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains
summary: Manufacturers often need to characterize a new material, process, or product before enough operating data are available to train reliable predictive models for this new, target domain. Existing manufacturing operations contain potentially useful knowledge to accelerate this characterization, but indiscriminate reuse of data from existing source domains can cause negative transfer in learning of the new, target domain when the manufacturing domains differ sufficiently. This work proposes a reinforcement-learning method for selective knowledge transfer, where its reward scores each opportunity to transfer against supervised alternatives, so negative transfer is avoided and controlled during forward prediction instead of being diagnosed afterwards. Given limited data from a new target domain, the learned policy chooses among predictors based on individual source operations, subsets of the sources, or the supervised alternatives: fully pooled sources, or target data alone. A validation gate deploys the transferred prediction only when it improves upon the supervised alternatives. The method is designed for learning variables supporting carbon accounting, as well as performance and quality outcomes. We demonstrate the approach by quantifying the embodied greenhouse-gas emissions of parts produced via material-extrusion additive manufacturing, using data from 729 experiments spanning five materials: ABS, PETG, TPU, PLA, and recycled PLA. The response combines measured fabrication electricity with polymer-specific cradle-to-gate production factors, while 22 material, process, and toolpath features characterize each experiment. In leave-one-material-out evaluation, this method achieves a mean test RMSE of 5.2 g CO2e per part, 20.00% lower than target-only training (32.5% lower when only 5-10% of the target training data are available) and 10.30% lower than indiscriminate source-target pooling.

title: SP$^2$ec: Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
summary: Speculative Decoding (SD) has demonstrated its efficacy in accelerating large language model inference, but for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the diverse input modalities make it difficult for a small trained drafter to achieve consistently high throughput. Self-speculative decoding reuses parts of the target model as a drafter which retains the multi-modal capability of the VLMs, yet its efficiency depends on choosing a suitable draft configuration for each prompt. We propose Single-Peak SPeculative decoding (SP$^2$ec), a training-free bandit algorithm that adapts the draft configuration during generation. SP$^2$ec exploits the single-peak throughput pattern observed in existing self-speculative methods, including SWIFT, KnapSpec, SpecVLM, and our simple cosSim. Our algorithmic design explicitly minimizes a novel notion of wall-time regret for each given query, corresponding to the empirical wall-time latency. Theoretical guarantees on the wall-time regret show that SP$^2$ec can exploit the optimal draft configuration, with negligible exploration cost. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B across visual and textual tasks show consistent improvements of up to 11\% over the original self-speculative methods, demonstrating the wide applicability of the proposed SP$^2$ec algorithm.

title: Enabling Token-wise Importance Sampling in Off-Policy RLVR with Proximal KL Regularization
summary: Off-policy data in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can arise from asynchronous generation, rollout-training mismatch, and response reuse. Token-wise importance weighting avoids multiplying likelihood ratios across a response but generally biases policy gradients. We prove that, under coverage and local expressiveness conditions, full future KL credit makes the exact proximal optimizer the update's unique stationary policy, even for mixtures of older policies, without full-response weights or a fitted critic. We further establish convergence of continuous-time tabular population updates under persistent coverage and time-varying behavior policies, and a finite-sample reward guarantee for linear logistic models under additional assumptions. These results motivate Proximal KL, a practical off-policy RLVR method that separates the proximal reference from the sampling policy and replaces PPO clipping with bounded future KL credit. Across all seven matched off-policy comparisons on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, spanning two learning rates, response reuse, and rollout staleness, Proximal KL outperforms GRPO in micro-averaged accuracy over eight math benchmarks by up to 2.58%. A separate on-policy comparison yields comparable aggregate accuracy. In periodic-refresh experiments, Proximal KL avoids the collapses observed in PG and CISPO, exceeds GRPO's training accuracy, and reaches higher accuracy in fewer policy updates. Ablations show that token-wise correction outperforms sequence-level and unweighted controls. With token-wise correction retained, future KL feedback reduces sensitivity to the tested baseline perturbation relative to PPO clipping. A finite future horizon improves AIME24 mean@16 and pass@16 over the full tail, while fixed-policy measurements show that truncation reduces correction variance over the tested horizons.

title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
summary: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.

title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

title: Depth Memory
summary: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.

title: Statistical Vignettes on the Grokking Phenomenon
summary: In this work, we study grokking in a simple, analytically tractable setting whose rich phenomenology allows us to disentangle the effects of initialization, signal strength, weight decay, sample size, and input dimension. These factors can produce superficially similar learning curves through distinct mechanisms, complicating their interpretation. Our analysis distinguishes early fitting through nuisance features, core feature learning, and delayed generalization. We identify sharp conditions under which grokking provably occurs and derive analytic asymptotic expressions for the lengths of the generalization plateaus. Our results also characterize regimes of early generalization and failure to reach a prescribed test accuracy target. We show that the interpolation edge constitutes a distinct dynamical regime, where vanishing spectral gaps separate core learning from generalization, helping clarify the role of proximity to interpolation in existing accounts of grokking. The resulting picture is analogous to fast and slow phases in chemical kinetics and suggests that the lazy-to-rich transition discussed in the literature may reflect a similar separation of dynamical time scales. Our theoretical results are faithfully supported by extensive experiments.

title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching
summary: A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance.

title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
summary: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.

title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
summary: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

title: Dependency, Compression, and Synergy: A Unified Information-Theoretic View of Multimodal Learning
summary: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have intensified the need to understand how different modalities share, preserve, and complement information. Mutual Information (MI), the Information Bottleneck (IB), and Partial Information Decomposition (PID) provide complementary perspectives, yet existing studies often treat them as isolated tools. This survey presents an information-theoretic perspective connecting these principles as progressively refined views of multimodal information processing: MI characterizes inter-modal dependency, IB explains task-oriented information preservation under compression, and PID decomposes preserved information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy. We review 170 recent studies (2018--2026) and 12 foundational works, organizing multimodal learning around four challenges: cross-modal alignment, information-efficient fusion, interaction-type characterization, and scaling to multimodal foundation models. Rather than using application domains as primary taxonomy axes, we interpret healthcare, robotics, recommendation systems, affective computing, and wireless communications as empirical validations of these information principles. Beyond taxonomy, we organize existing multimodal paradigms within a single information-theoretic coordinate system -- the Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian -- in which they occupy exact or approximate parameter corners, and whose unoccupied regions name candidate method families the literature has not yet built. We further discuss how emerging multimodal foundation models instantiate these principles at scale and identify open challenges including scalable information estimation in high-dimensional settings, standardized evaluation across information-theoretic methods, combinatorial complexity of multimodal PID, and the transition from post-hoc information analysis toward information-aware multimodal learning.

title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
summary:
Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories.
  It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.

title: Deep learning from a control vantage point
summary: This article offers an overview of recent developments in deep learning from a control vantage point. It reviews several classes of models including feedforward and residual neural networks, transformers, large-language models, and selective state space models while explaining how control theory plays an important role in understanding their training, properties, or architecture design. The article explains how residual neural networks can be interpreted as the discretization of a continuous-time control system thereby enabling the use of control theoretic techniques for its analysis. To illustrate the power of this bridge between control and deep learning, two technical results are discussed: 1) the ability of a residual neural network to approximate arbitrary continuous functions is a non-standard controllability problem that can be solved using geometric nonlinear control and 2) transformers, the key architectural component of most large language-models, can be seen the discretization of a consensus algorithm and thus large language-models exhibit consensus. Another point of contact between control theory and deep learning is the connection between backpropagation, the algorithm used to train neural networks, and optimal control. The article addresses how the older connection between these problems, established in the 80's using discrete-time models can be reconciled with the more recent approach using continuous-time models. Several open problems and directions for future research are discussed, including selective state-space models, a recent class of models inspired by the models used in control.

title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
summary: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.

title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
summary: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.

title: RF Fingerprinting of DSP Implementations using Machine Learning: An Over-the-Air Case Study
summary: Radio frequency fingerprinting aims to identify transmitters by exploiting small differences in the emitted signal waveform. Common approaches exploit hardware-dependent imperfections for that purpose. This work instead investigates whether differences between digital signal processing implementations of a transmitter can be identified from their radiated signals. As a practical case study, five different software-based DSP implementations for generating a 2-FSK RTTY communication waveform are considered. In a monitoring receiver, a classifier can identify these DSP implementations using convolutional neural networks that are trained on augmented software-generated signals represented as raw IQ, power spectrum or instantaneous frequency. The trained networks are evaluated on over-the-air recordings obtained using a shortwave transceiver and a software-defined radio receiver. The best neural network combines IQ and the power spectrum representation and achieves an accuracy of up to 90%. The study further examines the influence of the signal SNR and the observation bandwidth on the classification accuracy. The results demonstrate that DSP implementations leave distinguishable characteristics in the transmitted signals and suggest that DSP-dependent fingerprinting can provide complementary information for specific emitter identification systems.

title: Poisoned into Action: Context Attacks on Typed Decision Workflows
summary: Typed decision interfaces restrict models to predefined actions, yet schema-valid choices can still trigger policy-violating state changes. Evaluating context poisoning thus requires connecting model decisions to execution outcomes while accounting for legitimate automation retained by defenses. We introduce an execution-aware protocol tracing poisoned evidence through retrieval, model choice, automated action, and persisted state. We evaluate it with 1,659 fresh calls to Jev-1.13.0 across 20 development tasks in two synthetic workflows, using three repetitions per condition. Under natural retrieval, a standalone payload reaches all 60 trials and produces five security-violating executions, while a carrier-payload pair exposes the payload in 57 trials and produces one violation. An initial source-exclusion gate blocks the pair's observed violation but also withholds ten otherwise correct attacked decisions and sixteen correct clean decisions. Correcting its empty-scope behavior restores twelve clean decisions without additional model calls. Factorial controls show that adding correct evidence reduces wrong executions from 119/120 to 55/120 in the semantic arm and from 60/120 to zero in the neutral arm, suggesting that much of the improvement reflects general evidence value rather than attack-specific protection. Three prespecified contrasts are not statistically supported after Holm correction, so the findings remain exploratory. The protocol provides an auditable framework for studying which poisoning-induced errors reach execution and how much correct automation defenses preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/WuXixiong/jev-poisoning-bench.

title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
summary:
Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.
  We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.

title: Physics-guided machine learning for saturation control across variable hydraulic conditions in heap leaching
summary: Heap-leaching hydraulics vary between regions of an ore bed, motivating fast prediction models that accommodate different material properties. This study develops a parameter-conditioned physics-guided machine-learning (PGML) surrogate and demonstrates its use in simulated saturation control. A dataset of 4096 numerical Richards-equation trajectories was divided into 2867 training, 614 validation and 615 evaluation cases. The network predicts hourly saturation profiles from the current profile, irrigation rate and four hydraulic parameters, and is trained with an approximate Gardner mass-balance penalty. A daily predictive controller compared 200 constant irrigation rates over a 24-hour horizon. Across the evaluation cases, the median full-cycle tracking deviation was 4.9% of a 0.70 saturation target, equal to that of a tuned proportional-integral (PI) controller, while the PGML controller reached the target without overshoot in the median and applied approximately 4% less irrigation. Moderate physics guidance reduced long-horizon prediction error by approximately 30% relative to data-only training and reduced irrigation-bound activity, but slightly worsened closed-loop tracking. For a matched prediction workload, the surrogate was approximately 70 times faster than the numerical solver, and batched evaluation cost under 2 ms per column for 5000 columns. The results support a reusable physics-guided surrogate for large-scale saturation control in simulation.

title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
summary: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.

title: NetRL: Powering Network Decisions via NetGRPO-Driven Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Network decision-making tasks, including adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control, require
  policies to process heterogeneous states and actions while balancing near- and long-term consequences. Existing solutions
  generalize poorly across network tasks, require substantial task-specific redesign, and lack reliable evaluation of long-
  horizon action consequences. Methods that learn through online interaction additionally face unstable optimization. We
  present NetRL, a two-stage LLM-based reinforcement learning framework that combines supervised fine-tuning on
  demonstration trajectories with online policy optimization. A universal mixed-embedding interface combines textual task
  descriptions with precise numerical states, while a network action head produces valid decisions. At its core, NetGRPO
  evaluates candidate actions over multiple future trajectories, directs deeper search toward uncertain alternatives
  through confidence-aware budgeting, and performs group-relative, clipped, and KL-regularized updates. NetRL achieves
  23.6% higher QoE than NetLLM, 12.2% lower job completion time than Genet, and 24.1% higher network utility than Orca,
  yielding state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods. Confidence-aware budgeting reduces end-to-end training
  time by 27.1% without reducing validation QoE. NetRL also converges stably and generalizes to unseen network traces
  without retraining. Code and model weights are available at the repository linked in this paper.

title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
summary: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.

title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
summary: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.

title: Scalable Identification of Physics-Based and Neural Dynamics from Partial Measurements
summary: We present a scalable method for identifying nonlinear dynamics from partial measurements, supporting physics-based, neural-network, and gray-box models. We use the Prediction Error Method (PEM) coupled with state estimation performed by a Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) scheme, which can account directly for general nonlinear dynamics. This results in a bi-level optimization problem that scales poorly with increasing model parameters. To improve computational efficiency, we derive a reformulation that avoids explicit parameter-wide sensitivity matrices and exploits the temporal structure of the underlying optimization problem. Numerical comparisons show up to a $215\times$ speedup in hypergradient evaluation. Racing-vehicle simulations demonstrate accurate prediction and physical-parameter recovery in tire-force identification. Real-world data show that the gray-box model improves prediction accuracy with a neural residual while retaining physical interpretability.

title: RFWeave: Learning Wireless Propagation Across Scenes and Transceiver Configurations
summary: Wireless propagation modeling is foundational to the evaluation and design of modern communication systems. To achieve accurate wireless propagation prediction, recent learning-based approaches leverage scene geometry and materials, demonstrating promising generalization across transceiver locations and unseen scenes. However, these approaches remain largely confined to a fixed configuration of array size, receiver orientation, and transmit beam. In this work, we introduce RFWeave, a learned wireless propagation model designed to generalize across scenes, transceiver locations, and transceiver configurations. To accommodate varying array structures, RFWeave incorporates variable-length transceiver tokens that represent antenna elements individually. Furthermore, to capture the geometry between transmit and receive antenna elements, RFWeave aggregates their pairwise spatial relations into propagation tokens. A configuration-conditioned decoder predicts the spatial spectrum and received power. RFWeave is trained on a large-scale simulated dataset spanning 10,000 indoor scenes and more than 5 million channel records under diverse transceiver configurations. Extensive evaluations show that RFWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated generalization settings, improving spatial spectrum structural similarity (SSIM) by up to 15.7% and reducing received power mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 35.4% over the strongest baselines on unseen scenes. Additional experiments on measured DICHASUS data and in beam management further demonstrate RFWeave's broader applicability to real-world channels and downstream wireless tasks.

title: Universal Distributed Feature Extraction Complementary to Side Information via H-Score
summary: This paper considers a distributed estimation system where edge nodes transmit averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation. A key challenge arises when the center node possesses auxiliary side information: how to design local extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task, while avoiding redundancy with the side information. To tackle this problem, we orthogonally decompose the joint function space and demonstrate in the weak-dependence regime that the modal decomposition of the canonical dependence kernel's conditional-additive component yields optimal, task-independent features. We construct a distributed nested H-score to learn this decomposition and show that, under a limited feature budget, the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes, and vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.

title: Multi-Agent Deferred-Decision Trajectory Optimization with Anytime-Valid Target Retention for Moving Candidates
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
summary: We study multi-agent terminal interception when one of several moving candidates is the unknown target and both target identity and candidate terminal locations are uncertain. We develop a receding-horizon deferred-decision trajectory optimization (DDTO) controller that combines conformal terminal-location prediction, sequential candidate rejection, capacity-constrained assignment, and candidate-contingent planning. Under exchangeability conditions for terminal and identity residuals, with predictable querying, we establish fixed-time terminal-location coverage and anytime-valid target retention. At the final replan, when one control step remains, we bound the joint probability that a tightened-set DDTO plan passes nonlinear rollout verification but capture fails. The closed-loop controller applies fallback guidance to any agent without a verified DDTO plan and, across 100 paired scenarios, captures 79% of targets under the strict control-effort budget and 85% when that budget is relaxed.

title: Tight End-to-End Accounting for Differentially Private Synthetic Data
summary: Differentially private (DP) pipelines often combine heterogeneous mechanisms, yet their guarantees are best analyzed using different notions of privacy (e.g., bounded range, zCDP, ADP). When composing them, we have to analyze the guarantees through a reduced common representation that loses accounting precision. This issue is particularly relevant in DP synthetic data generation, where data preprocessing, generation algorithms, and DP-SGD could appear within the same pipeline. We develop novel tools for tight end-to-end accounting of such compositions using privacy loss distributions (PLD), $f$-DP, and Gaussian DP (GDP). In particular, we derive PLD and GDP analyses of bounded-range mechanisms such as the Exponential mechanism. Building on these theoretical results, we introduce AIM-GDP, a GDP-native variant of AIM (a state-of-the-art DP synthetic data mechanism) that enables easy composability with complex pipelines via PLD, attack-aware risk calibration, and tight end-to-end auditing while consistently achieving better utility; and MixCal, an algorithm for calibrating adaptive mixed compositions using PLD accounting. Overall, our tools enable tighter end-to-end accounting and thus less noise at the same privacy level in DP synthetic data pipelines.

title: Colored Graph Signal Diffusion Models
summary: Standard diffusion processes with isotropic noise corruption are not spectrally neutral. They inherit a coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy from the nonuniform data spectrum, because each frequency band loses signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at its own rate. For signals on a graph, the relevant spectrum is that of the graph shift operator (GSO). A natural construction, therefore, builds both the diffusion dynamics and the denoiser from graph filters of the GSO, and any such design also takes a position on this hierarchy. We expose this hierarchy as a tunable axis through a family of colored score-based diffusions. Fixing the terminal prior to a Gaussian colored by the GSO couples the drift and diffusion through a positive spectral rate, which acts as a clock for each graph-frequency band. The clock sets when a band loses and recovers information, and the forward processes of standard and certain graph-aware diffusions appear as members of this family. A GSO-valued EDM preconditioning splits the denoiser into an analytic Wiener head that carries the Gaussian second-order structure and a graph neural network (GNN) that learns the remaining non-Gaussian dependencies. Numerical experiments show that colored diffusions reach a given generation quality in far fewer sampling steps than standard diffusion.

title: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
summary: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.

title: CALM-5G: Event-Level Conformal Risk Control for Predictive Service-Assurance Alarms
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
summary: Predictive service assurance converts forecasts of key performance indicators into alarms, and that conversion decides whether the assurance function is deployable. We present CALM-5G, an assurance layer that operates above any forecasting backbone and issues alarms with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. It calibrates on service-level violation events, scores violation onset directly, selects its calibration scheme out of sample, and reports the alarm duty cycle with every certified miss rate.
